 What you need to know: Governor Newsom, in partnership with the Legislature, is helping Californians ditch Donald Trump’s high gas prices. Already, nearly 12,000 Californians have used the state’s MyFirstEV rebate program to save thousands of dollars switching to their first zero-emission vehicle. Despite the Trump administration’s attacks on American clean vehicle manufacturing and jobs, zero-emission vehicles accounted for nearly one in five new cars sold in California during the third quarter.

 SACRAMENTO – Governor Gavin Newsom today announced that nearly 12,000 Californians have switched to electric vehicles with MyFirstEV, the state’s instant rebate that gives first-time buyers $3,500 off a new zero-emission vehicle (ZEV) or $1,750 off a used one, right at the point of sale. 

 The milestone comes as ZEVs held strong at 19.1% of new car sales in California in the third quarter of 2026, and as U.S. electric vehicle sales climbed to their highest level in a year. Californians have now bought almost 2.8 million ZEVs, and more than 25,000 jobs have been announced in the state’s clean vehicle manufacturing and infrastructure industries.

 How MyFirstEV works

 Launched in August by Governor Newsom and the California Air Resources Board, California’s MyFirstEV rebate program takes the discount off at the point of sale, whether you buy at a dealership or directly from an automaker. There is no lengthy application period. The program stems from a $135.5 million investment by the Governor and the Legislature, matched dollar for dollar by participating automakers, delivering a combined $271 million in total savings to California families at the point of sale.

 Here’s what buyers need to know:

 $3,500 off new zero-emission vehicles with an MSRP up to $50,000

 $1,750 off used zero-emission vehicles sold for up to $25,000 through manufacturers’ pre-owned vehicle programs

 Open to any Californian buying their first ZEV .

 Rebates are still available through participating automakers , including Ford , General Motors , Honda , Hyundai , Kia , Lexus , Toyota , Lucid , Nissan , Rivian , Subaru , and Volvo . 

 “Californians are tired of skyrocketing gas prices. They also deserve a healthy environment and to breathe clean air, in addition to lower costs,” said Secretary for Environmental Protection Yana Garcia. “That’s why we will continue investing in innovative policies that protect Californians on multiple fronts: from their wallets to their health.”

 “California is full speed ahead. We’re cutting harmful vehicle pollution, delivering cleaner air, and building momentum — and the early success of MyFirstEV is supercharging that progress,” said California Air Resources Board Chair Lauren Sanchez. “Despite federal interference and attempts to turn back the clock, the global market is racing forward, and California will continue to lead.”

 Building on MyFirstEV’s early success, Toyota also recently launched its own privately funded offer to build on the Governor’s MyFirstEV program. Known as MyNextEV and MyLexusEV, these manufacturer-led programs give Californians who have owned an EV before an instant $2,500 off an eligible Toyota or Lexus electric car, whether they buy or lease. 

 California is racing to win, while Trump is asleep at the wheel

 Governor Newsom today announced California’s new 2026 Zero-Emission Vehicle Market Development Strategy , the next step in California’s plan to win the global ZEV economy. Developed by the Governor’s Office of Business and Economic Development (GO-Biz). This comprehensive, whole-of-government strategy serves as the state’s guiding framework for large-scale, equitable growth in the ZEV market and is structured around four core pillars – vehicles, infrastructure, end users, and workforce.

 “Zero-emission vehicles prove that what is good for our climate can also be good for our economy. They create good-paying jobs and catalyze economic development while cleaning our air and protecting our health,” said Dee Dee Myers, Senior Advisor to Governor Newsom and Director of the Governor’s Office of Business & Economic Development. “Now more than ever, we are committed to realizing our zero-emission future, and this strategy only further demonstrates that we have a clear and achievable path to get there.”

 The California Energy Commission (CEC) also released its latest EV charger assessment today, finding that California is already nearly halfway to meeting its projected 2030 charging needs. With 224,438 shared charging ports already installed statewide, California is nearly 50% of the way towards the 478,000 ports projected to support 6.8 million EVs by 2030. The report also highlights the significant economic opportunity ahead, with continued expansion of the state’s charging network supporting jobs in manufacturing, construction, and installation.

 “Despite the Trump administration’s continued attack on clean vehicles, California drivers continue to go electric, choosing EVs for a great driving experience and no more trips to the gas station,” said CEC Commissioner Nancy Skinner. “And MyFirstEV, the state’s EV purchase incentive program, is a great opportunity for drivers looking to join the trend and take advantage of California’s extensive network of publicly accessible EV charging infrastructure.” 

 California is in the fast lane as America’s #1 ZEV market. Under Governor Newsom, with support from the Legislature, the Golden State has invested nearly $6.6 billion since 2021 in ZEVs and the chargers powering them. Key highlights include:

 Jobs: More than 25,600 Californians work in ZEV manufacturing at 52 ZEV-related manufacturers based in California.

 Drivers: Californians have bought almost 2.8 million ZEVs . 

 Trucks : Nearly 1 in 4 new trucks, buses, and vans sold in California in 2024 were zero-emission, more than double the state’s target.

 EV Chargers: California has 224,438 public and limited-access charging ports , including about 23,000 fast chargers, plus almost 1.2 million estimated chargers at homes. Since 2021, fast charger installations have increased 221%.

 Regional growth : Six of California’s 13 Jobs First regions named ZEVs a priority growth industry, and 12 of the 13 named the clean economy a strategic sector. The state’s Jobs First economic blueprint puts ZEVs among the industries ready for new investment, bringing lasting good-paying jobs to communities across California.

 Drivers are tired of paying for Trump’s failed energy policies at the pump

 For too long, American families have paid for conflicts overseas every time they fill up. Trump’s reckless war in Iran is the latest bill — costing Americans nationwide more than $135 billion in extra fuel costs, amounting to over $1,000 per household. 

 The International Energy Agency says it caused the largest supply disruption in the history of the global oil market. While families paid more at the pump, oil and gas companies raked in $85.2 billion in profits in the second quarter of 2026, about $39 million every hour.

 Across the country, drivers are choosing electric in growing numbers, and the reasons are simple:

 Cheaper to fuel. Drivers save up to $2,000 per year on fuel alone by going electric.

 Cheaper to own. No oil changes, no spark plugs, no tune-ups, and regenerative braking that helps brake pads last longer.

 More choices. California drivers can pick from 145 light-duty EV models today. Before you buy, check which vehicles qualify for California’s MyFirstEV rebate program.

 No more price shocks . The cost of charging isn’t tied to volatile global oil markets prone to price spikes.

 SACRAMENTO – Governor Gavin Newsom today announced the following appointments:

 Michael Mullaney, of Sacramento, has been appointed Chief Policy Advisor to the President at the California Public Utilities Commission. Mullaney has been a Senior Advisor in the Office of the President at the California Public Utilities Commission since 2020. Mullaney was a Legislative Consultant in the Office of Governmental Affairs at the California Public Utilities Commission from 2017 to 2020. He held several positions in the Office of Governor Edmund G. Brown Jr. from 2013 to 2017, including Assistant Legislative Secretary and Legislative Assistant. Mullaney earned a Bachelor of Arts degree in History and Political Science from the University of California, Davis. This position does not require Senate confirmation and the compensation is $201,432. Mullaney is a Democrat.

 Cara Miyasaki, of San Jose, has been appointed to the Dental Board of California. Miyasaki was the Program Director at Foothill College from 1991 to 2023. She was Co-Owner of Tooth Fairy System from 2009 to 2017. Miyasaki was a Registered Dental Hygienist at Private Practice Offices from 2001 to 2015. She was a Registered Dental Assistant at Dental Fill-ins from 1983 to 1985. Miyasaki is a member of the Dental Assisting Council of the Dental Board of California, the California Dental Assisting Teachers Association, and the Northern California Golf Association. She earned a Master of Science degree in Oral Biology and a Bachelor of Science degree in Dental Hygiene from the University of California, San Francisco. This position does not require Senate confirmation, and the compensation is $100 per diem. Miyasaki is a Democrat.

 Kevin Cheng, of San Marino, has been reappointed to the Dental Board of California, where he has served since 2024. Cheng has been Director of Construction at City of Hope since 2021, where he was Senior Manager from 2017 to 2021. He was a Construction Manager at Shapell Properties Inc. from 2016 to 2017. Cheng was a Project Manager at Prestige Homes from 2013 to 2016. He was a Project Manager at TIS Construction Services, Inc. from 2009 to 2013. Cheng is a member of the Planning Commission at the City of San Marino. He earned a Juris Doctor degree from the University of Pacific, McGeorge School of Law and a Bachelor of Science degree in Business Administration from the University of California, Riverside. This position does not require Senate confirmation, and the compensation is $100 per diem. Cheng is registered without party preference.

 Ram Vaderhobli, of Belmont, has been reappointed to the Dental Board of California, where he has served since 2025. Vaderhobli has been a Clinical Professor of Preventive and Restorative Dental Sciences at the University of California, San Francisco School of Dentistry since 2020, where he has been Dental Director for the Advanced Education in General Dentistry program since 2010. He held multiple positions at the University of California, San Francisco School of Dentistry since 2007, including Health Sciences Assistant Clinical Professor, Health Sciences Associate Clinical Professor, and Clinical Director for Computer-Aided Design/Computer-Aided Manufacturing. Vaderhobli was California Regional Assistant Director for the Advanced Education in General Dentistry Program at Lutheran Medical Center from 2011 to 2015. He was a Resident in the Advanced Education in General Dentistry Program at the Eastman Institute for Oral Health of the University of Rochester from 2005 to 2006. Vaderhobli held multiple positions at the American Dental Association Paffenbarger Research Center from 2003 to 2004, including Research Specialist and Guest Scientist. He was a Research Assistant at Alfred University from 2002 to 2003. Vaderhobli is a Fellow of the American College of Dentists, International College of Dentists, and Pierre Fauchard Academy. He is a member of the American Association for Dental Research, the American Dental Education Association, the American Academy of Esthetic Dentistry, The Consortium for Oral Health Research and Informatics, and the Indian Dental Association. Vaderhobli earned a Master of Science degree in Biomaterials Engineering from Alfred University and a Bachelor of Dental Surgery degree from R.V. Dental College in India. This position does not require Senate confirmation, and the compensation is $100 per diem. Vaderhobli is registered without party preference.

 Monika Lee, of Sacramento, has been appointed to the Dental Hygiene Board of California. Lee has been Chief of Staff at the Office of Vice Mayor Karina Talamantes of the City of Sacramento since 2023. She was Senior Communications Strategist at Western Center on Law and Poverty in 2023. Lee was Senior Manager at Bryson Gillette from 2022 to 2023. She was an Associate Communications Director at California Pan-Ethnic Health Network from 2020 to 2022. Lee was Campaign Coordinator for Paschal Roth Public Affairs from 2018 to 2020. She was a Policy and Media Analyst at We Save Lives in 2017. Lee is a Board Member of the California Center for Civic Participation and Peachtree Health. Lee earned a Bachelor of Arts degree in Legal Studies from Scripps College. This position does not require Senate confirmation, and the compensation is $100 per diem. Lee is a Democrat.

 Sonia “Pat” Hansen, of Concord, has been reappointed to the Dental Hygiene Board of California, where she has served since 2022. Hansen has been a Registered Hygienist at Janis Richard DDS since 2013. She was the Lead Registered Dental Assistant at the Contra Costa County Sealant Program from 2002 to 2010. Hansen was a Registered Dental Assistant at the Contra Costa Dental Program from 2001 to 2010. She was reserve Police Officer at the Walnut Creek Police Department from 1992 to 2000. Hansen is a member of the California Dental Association, Community Dental Health Coordinators, and Walnut Festival. This position does not require Senate confirmation and the compensation is $100 per diem. Hansen is a Democrat.

 Sridevi Ponnala, of Fremont, has been reappointed to the Dental Hygiene Board, where she has served since 2023. Ponnala has been Chief Integration Officer at Tiburcio Vasquez Health Center since 2021, where she has held multiple positions since 2010, including Chief Dental Officer and Dental Director. She was an Adjunct Faculty in the Chabot Hygiene Program at the Chabot-Las Positas Community College District from 2016 to 2019. Ponnala was a Clinical Director at the Native American Health Center from 2007 to 2010. She earned a Doctor of Dental Surgery degree from the University of California, San Francisco School of Dentistry, a Master of Business Administration degree from California State University, East Bay, and a Bachelor of Dental Surgery degree from M.R. Ambedkar Dental College in India. This position does not require Senate confirmation, and the compensation is $100 per diem. Ponnala is a Democrat.

 Naleni Tribble-Agarwal, of Newark, has been reappointed to the Dental Hygiene Board of California, where she has served since 2023. Tribble-Agarwal has been a Dental Hygienist at Casey Herrera DDS since 2007. She was a Dental Hygienist at Marisa Walker DDS from 2014 to 2020. Tribble-Agarwal was a Dental Hygienist at Shital Kazi DDS from 2008 to 2018. She was a Dental Hygienist at Gurjit Randhawa DDS from 2008 to 2015. Tribble-Agarwal was a Dental Hygienist at Ross Stangeland DDS from 2008 to 2014. She was a Dental Hygienist at Richard Jenson DMD from 2008 to 2014. This position does not require Senate confirmation, and the compensation is $100 per diem. Tribble-Agarwal is a Democrat.

 Sherman King, of San Francisco, has been reappointed to the Dental Hygiene Board of California, where he has served since 2022. King was Chief Executive Officer at King Oasis LTD from 2010 to 2016. He was Director of Corporate Accounts at Infineon Technologies Inc. from 2000 to 2010. King was Applications Manager at AuraVision Inc. from 1991 to 1998. He was Principal Engineer at Western Digital Imaging Inc. from 1989 to 1991. King was Design Engineer at Advanced Micro Devices Inc. from 1983 to 1989. He was Office Manager at Eva Chau Acupuncture Clinic Office from 1982 to 2010. King is a board member of the San Francisco Chinatown Salvation Army, and a member of the Video Engineering Standards Association USA, the International Lions Club, the Chinese American Institute of Engineers and Scientists, and the Charity Cultural Services Center. He earned a Doctor of Philosophy degree in Business Administration from American Liberty University, a Master of Science degree in Electronic Engineering from Santa Clara University, and a Bachelor of Science degree in Electronic Engineering and Computer Science from the University of California, Berkeley. This position does not require Senate confirmation, and the compensation is $100 per diem. King is a Democrat.

 Denise Kadara, of Allensworth, has been reappointed to the Central Valley Regional Water Quality Control Board, where she has served since 2014. Kadara was a Senior Management Analyst and Economic Development Specialist for the City of San Mateo Community Development Department from 1997 to 2004. She was a Planning Committee Member of Tulare County Board of Supervisors for the 2nd District from 1994 to 1995. Kadara was a Senior Planner for the City of Hesperia Planning Department from 1990 to 1994. She was a Senior Planner and Administrative Analysts for the City of Fontana from 1986 to 1990. Kadara was a Project Coordinator for the City of Norwalk from 1984 to 1986. Kadara is a member of the ICARP Technical Advisory Committee and President of the Allensworth Progressive Association. This position requires Senate confirmation, and the compensation is $250 per diem. Kadara is a Democrat.

 Peter Satin, of Palm Desert, has been reappointed to the Colorado River Basin Regional Water Quality Control Board, where he has served since 2018. Satin has been Conservation Program Manager at Coachella Valley Association of Governments since 2023, where he was a Regional Planner from 2020 to 2022. Satin has held multiple positions at the Mojave Desert Land Trust including Director of Land Management from 2018 to 2020 and Land Stewardship Supervisor from 2017 to 2018. He was a Wildlife Technician at the United States Forest Service in 2016. Satin was a Community Health Educator at the Peace Corps from 2011 to 2014. He earned a Master of Environmental Management degree in Ecosystem Science and Conservation from Duke University and a Bachelor of Arts degree in Comparative Religion from Vassar College. This position requires Senate confirmation, and the compensation is $250 per diem. Satin is a Democrat. 

 Michael Mendez, of Los Angeles, has been reappointed to the Los Angeles Regional Water Quality Control Board, where he has served since 2021. Mendez has been an Associate Professor and Chancellor’s Fellow for Department of Urban Planning and Public Policy at the University of California at Irvine since 2025, where he was Assistant Professor from 2019 to 2025. He was a Faculty Fellow and Associate Research Scientist at Yale School of Forestry and Environment Studies from 2016 to 2019. Mendez was a Postdoctoral Scholar and Lecturer at University of San Francisco for Department of Environmental Science from 2015 to 2016. He was Legislative Director of State Governmental Relations at the University of California, Office of the President from 2008 to 2010. Mendez was a Senior Government Affairs Advocate for Blue Shield of California from 2006 to 2008. He was Senior Legislative Aide at the California State Assembly from 2003 to 2006. Mendez is a board member of the Public Policy Institute of California and Alliance for a Better Community. He earned a Doctor of Philosophy degree in Environmental Planning from the University of California, Berkeley, a Master of City and Environmental Planning degree from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, and a Bachelor of Arts degree in Urban and Environmental Planning from California State University, Northridge. This position requires Senate confirmation, and the compensation is $250 per diem. Mendez is a Democrat.

 SAN FRANCISCO – Governor Gavin Newsom and Monique Barbut, France’s Minister for the Ecological Transition, Biodiversity, and International Climate and Nature Negotiations, signed a letter of intent launching a new partnership to strengthen cooperation on clean energy, climate resilience, and environmental protection, while creating opportunities for research, innovation, trade, and economic development.

 The partnership brings California and France together around a practical goal: sharing what works to better protect people from climate change and strengthen their economies. Both face climate-driven realities, including destructive wildfires, drought, flooding, and extreme heat.

 Turning shared challenges into practical solutions 

 The partnership establishes a framework for cooperation across climate action and environmental protection. Priority areas include:

 Protecting communities from wildfire and extreme heat. California and France will share approaches to preventing and reducing wildfire impacts and heat-related illnesses, helping both partners learn from the challenges their communities face.

 Boost clean energy and strengthen electric grids. The partnership will facilitate exchanges among France’s electricity transmission operator and California’s energy agencies and grid operator. Cooperation will also explore artificial intelligence’s impact on electricity demand and how AI can help modernize grids as well as improving energy efficiency in buildings.

 Advancing cleaner transportation. The partnership supports exchanges on reducing transportation pollution, including through high-speed rail.

 Supporting agriculture and protecting nature. Cooperation will also focus on climate-smart agriculture, agricultural technology, sustainable pest management, and nature-based solutions. Both partners share a goal of conserving 30% of their lands and coastal waters by 2030.

 Reducing pollution and waste. The partnership will support cooperation on air quality, cutting greenhouse gas emissions, including methane, and approaches that keep materials in use and reduce waste.

 Connecting businesses and researchers to economic opportunity

 The new partnership will promote connections among government, businesses, and researchers to support innovation, deepen trade and commercial ties, and advance economic development.

 The Letter of Intent calls for exchanges of ideas between the California Governor’s Office of Business and Economic Development and the Consulate General of France in San Francisco, alongside public-private partnerships focused on climate and environmental solutions, including clean energy technologies. These connections and engagements are intended to support researchers and businesses in finding partners and moving promising ideas toward practical use.

 California’s global climate network 

 California has long been a key player on the international stage — from taking joint action on climate change to identifying new pathways and partnerships for sustained economic growth. During the Newsom administration alone, California has formed over 70 international partnerships that lay critical groundwork for our continued economic success, while prioritizing workers and businesses that benefit from these new opportunities.

 Golden State and global partnerships 

 Finland (2026): California and Finland signed a memorandum of understanding to deepen economic cooperation and advance clean technology, innovation, and sustainable growth. The partnership connects businesses, researchers, and governments through collaboration on quantum computing, cybersecurity, health and life sciences, aerospace, and sustainable forest-based industries.

 Spain (2026): California and Spain signed a memorandum of understanding to advance clean energy, strengthen energy security, and prepare communities for climate impacts. Cooperation spans renewable energy, electrification, battery storage, carbon markets, methane reduction, and grid reliability, with a shared commitment to protecting communities from extreme heat and wildfire and benefiting workers and businesses.

 United Kingdom (2026): California and the United Kingdom signed a memorandum of understanding to tackle climate change and promote sustainable development together. The memorandum of understanding builds on an already strong history of cooperation, and focuses on areas for collaboration including clean energy technologies, climate resilience, decarbonizing transportation, and protecting the natural environment. 

 Chile (2025): California and Chile signed a memorandum of understanding regarding exchanging information, developing best practices, and cooperating on methane emissions reduction. Methane is a highly potent greenhouse gas, and the partnership between California and Chile opens up new opportunities for both partners to cooperate on methane reduction in waste, agriculture, and energy sectors.

 Colombia (2025): California and Colombia signed a partnership to advance joint efforts on forest conservation , methane reduction, climate resilience, and clean energy development. The memorandum of understanding deepens coordination on protecting the Amazon, strengthening biodiversity, and expanding nature-based climate solutions that support sustainable and equitable economic growth.

 Nigeria (2025): California signed a memorandum of understanding with Nigeria on sustainable urban transportation, green ports, low-carbon transportation fuels, climate adaptation, methane detection and abatement policies, greenhouse gas emissions and air quality, and academic exchange and university partnerships. The partnership will build upon our shared commitment to sustainable growth, accelerate the transition to zero-emission transportation, and expand opportunities for the next generation.

 Brazil (2025): California signed a memorandum of understanding with the Brazilian federal government to scale up cooperation on climate, clean energy, cutting pollution, and job-creating climate opportunities. This new partnership, announced in September 2025, will advance market-based carbon pricing programs, expand clean transportation, including zero-emission vehicles and low-carbon fuels, and strengthen air quality management through enhanced monitoring and regulatory controls. The partnership also focuses on conserving 30% of lands and coastal waters by 2030, including nature-based solutions and biodiversity protection. In 2025, California also advanced a partnership with the State of Pará to strengthen cooperation on wildfire prevention and response — enhancing forest monitoring, identifying areas most at risk, and sharing research and expertise to improve firefighting and emergency management. 

 Kenya (2025): California signed a partnership focused on cutting pollution and supporting trade. The partnership advances medium- and long-term low-carbon development , policy research, development, and innovation in sustainable land use and urban planning that reduces long commutes and urban sprawl, while promoting integrated land use and transport systems. 

 Noord-Holland (2024): California and Noord-Holland signed a Letter of Intent advancing next-generation air mobility — from drones to zero-emission aircraft. Joint innovation missions are producing pilot projects that inform California’s Advanced Air Mobility Implementation Plan and readiness for major global events.

 Australia (2023): California signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) with Australia that helped inform the country’s first-ever vehicle carbon emissions standards through input from the California Air Resources Board. The California Public Utilities Commission and California ISO have also advised Australia on electricity market reform to better align incentives for renewable energy.

 British Columbia (2023): California and British Columbia signed a memorandum of understanding on mutual wildfire assistance that is delivering results. British Columbia sent incident management experts to support California’s Palisades Fire in 2025, while CAL FIRE deployed personnel during British Columbia’s 2025 fire season. These exchanges established a lasting framework for cross-border wildfire support.

 China (2023): California signed five Memoranda of Understanding (MOUs) with China’s National Development and Reform Commission, the provinces of Guangdong and Jiangsu, and the municipalities of Beijing and Shanghai to advance cooperation in cutting greenhouse gas emissions, transitioning away from fossil fuels, and developing clean energy.

 Denmark (2021): California and Denmark signed a memorandum of understanding to collaborate on groundwater mapping, leak detection, and water efficiency, which has modernized California’s data systems and informed key state programs, like the Airborne Electromagnetic Survey. Danish technologies and expertise have helped strengthen drought and water-supply resilience statewide.

 Mexico (Baja California & Sonora): California signed Memoranda of Understanding (MOUs) with the Mexican states of Baja California and Sonora to advance zero-emission freight corridors, clean ports, and battery manufacturing — strengthening North American supply chains and workforce readiness. Joint forums have already produced new research collaborations and training programs advancing clean-tech.

 California’s clean energy leadership 

 Since Governor Newsom took office in 2019, California has added more than 37,000 megawatts of utility-scale clean and renewable energy to serve the California grid — and battery storage has ramped up from fewer than 700 MW to more than 21,000 MW , helping make the grid more reliable and pushing the state further along its clean energy transition.

 Batteries play a key role in California’s goal of getting all of its electricity from clean sources by 2045. The most recent numbers, from the end of 2024, show real progress: 67% of retail electricity sales in the state already come from clean energy. Last year, clean energy met 100% of the state’s electricity needs for at least part of the day on 279 separate days. So far in 2026, that’s happened on more than nine out of 10 days during the first half of the year.

 Clean energy is also good for the economy. California leads the nation in total clean energy jobs, with 552,300 workers employed across clean energy technologies, nearly twice as many as the second-ranked state, Texas, according to a 2025 report from E2 . California’s clean energy workforce grew by nearly 7,300 workers in 2024, outpacing job growth in the rest of the state’s economy by more than three times.

This year, California enacted new protections and investments to continue to safeguard elections and defend democracy — strengthening trust in the outcome of the elections here in California.

 Given changes to the U.S. Postal Service under the Trump administration, Californians who plan to return their ballot by mail should do so at least a week before Election Day.

 California elected leaders across the state are standing together to ensure every vote counts. From my office to your local county registrar, we are committed to making sure every eligible voter is able to exercise their civic duty. Know your voting rights. Take time to review what’s on your ballot, and VOTE EARLY,” said California Secretary of State Shirley N. Weber Ph.D. “Staying informed turns confusion into clarity and clarity into power.Your voice is what helps move our communities forward.” 

 “We are just four weeks from Election Day, and I know some Californians may be wondering whether everything coming out of Washington has changed how they can vote. The answer is no,” said Attorney General Bonta . “We successfully secured a U.S. Supreme Court order that protects your ability to vote by mail, so you can continue to vote as you have in past elections —whether by mail, ballot drop box, early, or in-person on Election Day. My fellow attorneys general and I have been in close contact and are ready to take action against any new attempt to undermine voters’ rights. With ballots beginning to arrive, I encourage everyone to vote early to ensure your voice is heard.” 

 Information about voting in California 

 If you are unsure if you are registered to vote, you can visit this site to learn more. If you are not registered to vote and are eligible to do so , you have until October 19th to register. Eligible voters who miss that deadline can still register to vote on election day through California’s Conditional Voter Registration . 

 IMPORTANT REMINDER: Under the U.S. Postal Service’s new process , mail dropped off at post offices and mail collection boxes more than 50 miles from a U.S. Postal Service regional hub is collected the next day, instead of the same day. This means that, in some areas, ballots dropped off at a post office or mail collection box on Election Day won’t be postmarked until the day after, making them late. Late ballots are not counted. Californians who plan to return their ballot by mail should do so at least a week before Election Day.

 Alternative ways to ensure your vote is counted instead of using the U.S. Postal Service:

 Drop off your ballot at a secure ballot drop-off box or vote center . Ballot drop-off boxes are now open and remain available until Election Day.

 If you’re cutting it close, drop off your completed mail ballot at a vote center on Election Day — do not put it in the mail, it may not be counted.

 Go to any post office and ask at the counter for a postmark on your ballot to ensure you get credit for mailing your ballot on time.

 The rights available to the public when voting are listed in the California Voter Bill of Rights . Denial of any of these rights can be reported in English through the Secretary of State’s confidential toll-free Voter Hotline at (800) 345-VOTE (8683). Other language options, including Spanish, Tagalog, and Chinese, are available. In addition, reports can be made via email at elections@sos.ca.gov . 

 Voters can track their ballot throughout the electoral process at WheresMyBallot.com .

 New protections in place 

 Last month, Governor Newsom signed 13 new laws to safeguard California election process from potential meddling — including from federal officials — created new felonies to hold those accountable for any attempts to disrupt the electoral process in the state, and continued to advance efforts to increase participation by eligible voters. Earlier this year, the Governor took action to defend democracy ahead of the primary elections in the state, signing SB 73 into law.

 Key investments made this year 

 In his final budget, the Governor and Legislature included several key investments in the state’s election system:

 $29 million for increased staffing, technology and equipment upgrades and purchases for counties to speed up counting and increase capacity.

 $5 million for voter outreach and education at the county level to help Californians know resources and tools available in their community.

 $5 million for voter outreach and education at the statewide level via the office of Secretary of State.

 $750,000 to support statewide efforts to combat mis- and disinformation and ensure the state is prepared to guard against federal interference.

 A long record of defending democracy 

 In addition to the 14 bills signed this year to defend democracy, last year, Governor Newsom signed :

 SB 3 (Cervantes) — requires that public vote counts are updated more regularly and made changes to the signature curing process for vote by mail ballots.

 SB 42 (Umberg) — puts on the November 2026 ballot a measure to repeal the ban on public financing of elections in California, extending to all cities and counties the ability to create programs for publicly financed elections, helping level the playing field for candidates and reducing the ability of millionaires and billionaires to essentially buy elections.

 SB 398 (Umberg) — criminalizes offering payments and other valuable items to incentivize voting or voter registration. The bill defines “other valuable consideration” to include a chance to win a lottery or prize-drawing contest. The crime would be punishable by imprisonment, a fine of up to $10,000, or both fine and imprisonment. 

 AB 5 (Berman) — requires election officials to finish counting all ballots by the 13th day following Election Day unless certain conditions are met.

 AB 16 (Alanis) — extended the time before the election date that vote by mail ballots can be processed. 

 In 2024, Governor Newsom signed : 

 AB 2655 (Berman) — requires large online platforms to remove or label deceptive and digitally altered or created content related to elections during specified periods, and requires them to provide mechanisms to report such content. It also authorizes candidates, elected officials, elections officials, the Attorney General, and a district attorney or city attorney to seek injunctive relief against a large online platform for noncompliance with the act.

 AB 2839 (Pellerin) — expands the timeframe in which a committee or other entity is prohibited from knowingly distributing an advertisement or other election material containing deceptive AI-generated or manipulated content. The bill also expands the scope of existing law to prohibit materially deceptive content of elected officials, candidates, elections officials and others, authorizing them to file a civil action to enjoin the distribution of such material.

 AB 2355 (Carrillo) — requires that electoral advertisements using AI-generated or substantially altered content feature a disclosure that the material has been altered. The bill authorizes the Fair Political Practices Commission to enforce a violation of these disclosure requirements by seeking injunctive relief to compel compliance or pursuing other remedies available to the commission under the Political Reform Act.

 This builds on Governor Newsom’s prior work: In 2021, he signed 10 bills into law to safeguard elections and increase access so more Californians can lawfully participate; in 2020, the Governor took several actions ( here , here , here ) to ensure Californians could participate despite the ongoing global pandemic; and in 2019, Governor Newsom signed more than 17 bills into law to defend democracy — including some of the nation’s first that address deepfakes.

 California at Climate Week NYC

 Climate Week NYC convenes government leaders, businesses, investors, advocates, researchers, philanthropies, and community leaders from around the world to advance practical climate solutions. 

 Governor Newsom participated to highlight California’s record of cutting pollution while growing the economy, strengthen partnerships with international and subnational leaders, and accelerate progress on clean energy, zero-emission transportation, climate resilience, and economic opportunity. In addition, leaders from throughout state government represented California at a number of events and programs, including the announcement of new programs and partnerships.

 CNRA Secretary Wade Crowfoot participates in a subnational leaders roundtable on best practices for achieving global climate goals. 

 In New York, California Secretary for Natural Resources Wade Crowfoot participated in the Under2 Coalition’s Governor’s Dialogue on Subnational Leadership and the America Is All In and U.S. Climate Alliance meeting with UN Framework Convention on Climate Change Executive Secretary Simon Stiell. These discussions provided the opportunity for subnational leaders in the United States and around the world to share best practices for achieving global climate goals and demonstrate continued American climate action. 

 Secretary Crowfoot also met with key international partners in New York for Climate Week, including Quebec, Catalonia, and the Western Cape. Discussions focused on how to best prepare for worsening droughts and floods, protect residents during heat waves, and create cleaner and more affordable energy for residents. 

 Finally, the Secretary showcased California’s leadership on adapting to new weather realities and climate impacts, scaling nature-based solutions and accelerating action through international partnerships at events organized by The Climate Registry, The Rocky Mountain Institute, and more.

 Secretary Yana Garcia gave remarks at the Subnational Methane Action Coalition’s “The Super Pollutant Sprint” in New York at Climate Week 2026, where Catalonia joined the coalition. 

 At Climate Week NYC, California’s Secretary for Environmental Protection (CalEPA), Yana Garcia, joined dynamic panels, high-level convenings, and bilateral meetings to highlight California’s leadership in environmental and public health protection. 

 The Secretary kicked off Climate Week at the California Climate Leadership Forum, highlighting the state’s climate progress — including the Cap-and-Invest program, MyFirstEV, and energy infrastructure investments — before joining other programming on regenerative farming, zero-emissions transportation, electric innovation, and cutting super pollutant emissions. She also gave key remarks at the Subnational Methane Coalition’s “Hub Live: Super Pollutant Sprint,” where Catalonia joined the coalition that California co-founded.

 Secretary Garcia also highlighted California’s progress on zero-emission transportation across both consumer and commercial/freight sectors to cut marine-sector air pollution alongside the Port of Long Beach, and closed Climate Week representing the state at the “Friends of Kigali” event in support of the Kigali Amendment’s commitments to resilient cooling and reduced super pollutants. 

 CARB advances California climate leadership at Climate Week NYC

 California Resources Board (CARB) Chair Lauren Sanchez began the week by joining former CARB Chair Mary Nichols for a panel on California’s Climate Disclosure program, highlighting how the state is filling a federal gap left by the stalled U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) climate disclosure rule. She then participated in an Under2 Coalition roundtable on strengthening information resilience for the climate and energy transition. 

 On Tuesday, she discussed California’s recent climate progress and the importance of subnational coordination with International Emissions Trading Association CEO Dirk Forrester, followed by a panel at the Electric Innovation Forum with leaders from Maryland, Long Beach, and Delaware on leveraging private investment for electrification, moderated by New York Times energy correspondent Ivan Penn. She concluded the day by taking part in a conversation about this year’s Cap‑and‑Invest rulemaking and how program updates will support climate goals while maintaining affordability.

 The Chair also participated in several events hosted by the Electric Innovation Initiative, including a roundtable of governors, state legislators, and mayors to discuss electrification of vehicle fleets and buildings; and an award ceremony highlighting electrification advancements across the United States. 

 CDFA highlights California’s agricultural economy

 While attending New York Climate Week, Secretary Karen Ross, of the California Department of Food and Agriculture (CDFA), signed a Memorandum of Understanding with Catalonia, Spain, establishing a strengthened framework for collaboration between the two regions as they face similar agricultural challenges driven by climate change. 

 Secretary Ross also participated in a panel hosted by the Climate Registry, highlighting California’s commitment to innovation and AgTech as critical tools for meeting the state’s climate targets. In addition, she joined discussions hosted by Food Tank and the Ag Policy Forum, where she underscored the growing challenges facing farmers and reaffirmed CDFA’s priority of fostering a climate-smart, resilient, and regenerative food system. Secretary Ross also attended a lunch celebrating the Farm-to-School program’s monumental achievements and the lasting impact it will have on farmers and families for generations to come thanks to the recently secured ongoing funding.

 California’s keeping the climate conversation going

 During Climate Week NYC, the California Governor’s Office of Land Use and Climate Innovation (LCI) held a virtual event, “ International Heat Solutions: Through a California Lens ,” which highlighted California’s bold investments to reduce heat risks and brought together international leaders to share solutions, inspire collaboration, and accelerate action on extreme heat. 

 California’s global climate network

 California has long been a key player on the international stage — from taking joint action on climate change to identifying new pathways and partnerships for sustained economic growth. During the Newsom administration alone, California has formed over 70 international partnerships that lay critical groundwork for our continued economic success, while prioritizing workers and businesses that benefit from these new opportunities.

 Golden State and global partnerships 

 Finland (2026) : This year at Climate Week NYC, California and Finland signed a partnership to create a framework for collaboration on clean technology and sustainability, aerospace and defense innovation, health and life sciences, emerging technologies, quantum computing, cybersecurity, research, and sustainable forest bioeconomy. The partnership calls for the exchange of policy ideas and best practices, support for research collaborations, promotion of business engagement, and stronger relationships among California and Finnish local and regional jurisdictions. 

 Germany (2026) : California and Germany pledged to strengthen climate cooperation , emphasizing that climate change and environmental degradation threaten global security and economic stability. The two leaders pledged deeper cooperation on green/renewable technologies that cut pollution while creating jobs and economic growth. 

 United Kingdom (2026) : California and the United Kingdom signed a memorandum of understanding to tackle climate change and promote sustainable development together. The memorandum of understanding builds on an already strong history of cooperation, and focuses on areas for collaboration including clean energy technologies, climate resilience, decarbonizing transportation, and protecting the natural environment. 

 Chile (2025) : California and Chile signed a memorandum of understanding to exchange information, develop best practices, and cooperate on methane emissions reduction. Methane is a highly potent greenhouse gas, and the partnership between California and Chile opens up new opportunities for both partners to cooperate on methane reduction in waste, agriculture, and energy sectors.

 Colombia (2025) : California and Colombia signed a partnership to advance joint efforts on forest conservation , methane reduction, climate resilience, and clean energy development. The memorandum of understanding deepens coordination on protecting the Amazon, strengthening biodiversity, and expanding nature-based climate solutions that support sustainable and equitable economic growth.

 Nigeria (2025) : California signed a memorandum of understanding with Nigeria on sustainable urban transportation, green ports, low-carbon transportation fuels, climate adaptation, methane detection and abatement policies, greenhouse gas emissions and air quality, and academic exchange and university partnerships. The partnership will build upon our shared commitment to sustainable growth, accelerate the transition to zero-emission transportation, and expand opportunities for the next generation.

 Brazil (2025) : California signed a memorandum of understanding with the Brazilian federal government to scale up cooperation on climate, clean energy, cutting pollution, and job-creating climate opportunities. This new partnership, announced in September 2025, will advance market-based carbon pricing programs, expand clean transportation, including zero-emission vehicles and low-carbon fuels, and strengthen air quality management through enhanced monitoring and regulatory controls. The partnership also focuses on conserving 30% of lands and coastal waters by 2030, including nature-based solutions and biodiversity protection. In 2025, California also advanced a partnership with the State of Pará to strengthen cooperation on wildfire prevention and response — enhancing forest monitoring, identifying areas most at risk, and sharing research and expertise to improve firefighting and emergency management. 

 Kenya (2025) : California signed a partnership focused on cutting pollution and supporting trade. The partnership advances medium- and long-term low-carbon development , policy research, development, and innovation in sustainable land use and urban planning that reduces long commutes and urban sprawl, while promoting integrated land use and transport systems. 

 Noord-Holland (2024) : California and Noord-Holland signed a Letter of Intent advancing next-generation air mobility — from drones to zero-emission aircraft. Joint innovation missions are producing pilot projects that inform California’s Advanced Air Mobility Implementation Plan and readiness for major global events.

 Australia (2023) : California signed a memorandum of understanding with Australia that helped inform the country’s first-ever vehicle emissions standards through input from the California Air Resources Board. The California Public Utilities Commission and California ISO have also advised Australia on electricity market reform to better align incentives for renewable energy.

 British Columbia (2023) : California and British Columbia signed a memorandum of understanding on mutual wildfire assistance that is delivering results. British Columbia sent incident management experts to support California’s Palisades Fire in 2025, while CAL FIRE deployed personnel during British Columbia’s 2025 fire season. These exchanges established a lasting framework for cross-border wildfire support.

 China (2023) : California signed five memoranda of understanding with China’s National Development and Reform Commission, the provinces of Guangdong and Jiangsu, and the municipalities of Beijing and Shanghai to advance cooperation in cutting greenhouse gas emissions, transitioning away from fossil fuels, and developing clean energy.

 Denmark (2021) : California and Denmark signed a memorandum of understanding to collaborate on groundwater mapping, leak detection, and water efficiency, which has modernized California’s data systems and informed key state programs, like the Airborne Electromagnetic Survey. Danish technologies and expertise have helped strengthen drought and water-supply resilience statewide.

 Mexico (Baja California & Sonora) : California signed memoranda of understanding with the Mexican states of Baja California and Sonora to advance zero-emission freight corridors, clean ports, and battery manufacturing — strengthening North American supply chains and workforce readiness. Joint forums have already produced new research collaborations and training programs advancing clean-tech.

 California’s clean energy leadership

 Since Governor Newsom took office in 2019, California has added more than 37,000 megawatts of utility-scale clean and renewable energy to serve the California grid — and battery storage has ramped up from fewer than 700 MW to more than 21,000 MW , helping make the grid more reliable and pushing the state further along its clean energy transition.

 Batteries play a key role in California’s goal of getting all of its electricity from clean sources by 2045. The most recent numbers, from the end of 2024, show real progress: 67% of retail electricity sales in the state already come from clean energy. Last year, clean energy met 100% of the state’s electricity needs for at least part of the day on 279 separate days. So far in 2026, that’s happened on more than nine out of 10 days during the first half of the year.

 Clean energy is also good for the economy. California leads the nation in total clean energy jobs, with 552,300 workers employed across clean energy technologies, nearly twice as many as the second-ranked state, Texas, according to a 2025 report from E2 . California’s clean energy workforce grew by nearly 7,300 workers in 2024, outpacing job growth in the rest of the state’s economy by more than three times.

 Expanding California’s carbon market

 Governor Newsom joined Dr. Champa Patel, Executive Director for Governments and Policy at Climate Group, for a fireside conversation at the North America Climate Summit hosted by the International Emissions Trading Association, where he announced California’s move towards linking its pioneering carbon market with Washington State. As we continue advancing towards our climate goals, linking our program with other jurisdictions can make the program even stronger and more durable, while also expanding opportunities for many industries to reduce their emissions even more cost-effectively. 
 This summer, Governor Newsom delivered $886 million in utility-bill relief through the California Climate Credit, which returns Cap-and-Invest proceeds to residential customers. Millions of California households received an average $75 credit on their electricity bills. Between now and 2030, the program is expected to generate $10 billion in electric bill credits, putting money directly back into Californians’ pockets while holding polluters accountable for their emissions. 

 California’s Cap-and-Invest program, thirteen years in, has generated $37 billion in climate investments, supporting 143,000 good-paying jobs and cutting millions of tons of carbon emissions. 

 California’s Cap-and-Invest Program is part of the larger suite of programs the state has been deploying for two decades to address climate pollution. It establishes a declining limit on emissions from the largest polluters, including large factories, energy companies, and oil and gas suppliers, accounting for 80% of the state’s total climate emissions, and requires polluters who go beyond this limit to invest in projects to benefit Californians.

 Deepening California-Australia cooperation

 Governor Newsom met with Australian Ambassador to the United States Greg Moriarty and officials from Australia’s Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water Ministry to discuss expanding the California-Australia collaboration on energy security, affordability, climate resilience, battery storage, zero-emission transportation, and sharing best practices on the challenges and opportunities of emerging technologies. The leaders also discussed Australia’s COP31 priorities and opportunities to demonstrate practical climate implementation on the global stage. 
 California and Australia have partnered through a 2023 Memorandum of Understanding on work ranging from grid innovation and energy storage to water-quality monitoring and critical-minerals research.

 Launching California-Finland partnership

 Governor Newsom inked a new partnership with Finnish Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen to strengthen California-Finland economic cooperation and advance a sustainable, inclusive green economy. The partnership creates a framework for collaboration on clean technology and sustainability, aerospace and defense innovation, health and life sciences, emerging technologies, quantum computing, cybersecurity, research, and sustainable forest bioeconomy. 
 “California and Finland are global leaders in innovation, sustainability, and the industries shaping the future,” said Dee Dee Myers, Director of the Governor’s Office of Business and Economic Development. “This new partnership will help deepen economic cooperation and create new opportunities to advance clean energy, emerging technologies, and sustainable growth.”

 “Finland is proud to partner with a state that shares our ambition to develop solutions for the future,” said Elina Valtonen, Minister for Foreign Affairs of Finland. “This partnership deepens cooperation between Finland and California, creates new economic opportunities, and strengthens collaboration and dialogue on innovation and emerging technologies across the Atlantic.”

 The partnership calls for the exchange of policy ideas and best practices, support for research collaborations, promotion of business engagement, and stronger relationships among California and Finnish local and regional jurisdictions.

 California and Finland share interests in clean technology, methane reduction, climate resilience, and innovation.

 United Nations climate action

 At the United Nations, Governor Newsom called out Donald Trump for abandoning America’s responsibility to confront the climate crisis and protect the strongest economy in the world. The Governor joined local and regional leaders from around the world at the United Nations Secretary-General’s High-level Event on Climate Action and the Just Transition , underscoring that subnational governments remain essential partners in confronting the climate crisis. As the highest-ranking U.S. voice on the panel, the Governor highlighted California’s record of pairing climate action with economic growth, and he reaffirmed the Golden State’s commitment to working with global partners to accelerate the clean energy transition. 

 The Governor joined Freetown Mayor Aki-Sawyerr, Boston Mayor Michelle Wu, Western Cape Premier Alan Winde, and former Paris Mayor Anne Hidalgo in the session’s only panel of subnational leaders. During the panel, Governor Newsom underscored the importance of subnational governments delivering practical climate solutions at speed and scale.

 California at Climate Week NYC

 Climate Week NYC convenes government leaders, businesses, investors, advocates, researchers, philanthropies, and community leaders from around the world to advance practical climate solutions. 
 Governor Newsom is participating to highlight California’s record of cutting pollution while growing the economy, strengthen partnerships with international and subnational leaders, and accelerate progress on clean energy, zero-emission transportation, climate resilience, and economic opportunity.

 California’s global climate network

 California has long been a key player on the international stage — from taking joint action on climate change to identifying new pathways and partnerships for sustained economic growth. During the Newsom administration alone, California has formed over 70 international partnerships that lay critical groundwork for our continued economic success, while prioritizing workers and businesses that benefit from these new opportunities. 
 Golden State and global partnerships 

 United Kingdom (2026): California and the United Kingdom signed a memorandum of understanding to tackle climate change and promote sustainable development together. The memorandum of understanding builds on an already strong history of cooperation, and focuses on areas for collaboration including clean energy technologies, climate resilience, decarbonizing transportation, and protecting the natural environment. 

 Chile (2025): California and Chile signed a memorandum of understanding regarding exchanging information, developing best practices, and cooperating on methane emissions reduction. Methane is a highly potent greenhouse gas, and the partnership between California and Chile opens up new opportunities for both partners to cooperate on methane reduction in waste, agriculture, and energy sectors.

 Colombia (2025): California and Colombia signed a partnership to advance joint efforts on forest conservation , methane reduction, climate resilience, and clean energy development. The memorandum of understanding deepens coordination on protecting the Amazon, strengthening biodiversity, and expanding nature-based climate solutions that support sustainable and equitable economic growth.

 Nigeria (2025): California signed a memorandum of understanding with Nigeria on sustainable urban transportation, green ports, low-carbon transportation fuels, climate adaptation, methane detection and abatement policies, greenhouse gas emissions and air quality, and academic exchange and university partnerships. The partnership will build upon our shared commitment to sustainable growth, accelerate the transition to zero-emission transportation, and expand opportunities for the next generation.

 Brazil (2025): California signed a memorandum of understanding with the Brazilian federal government to scale up cooperation on climate, clean energy, cutting pollution, and job-creating climate opportunities. This new partnership, announced in September 2025, will advance market-based carbon pricing programs, expand clean transportation, including zero-emission vehicles and low-carbon fuels, and strengthen air quality management through enhanced monitoring and regulatory controls. The partnership also focuses on conserving 30% of lands and coastal waters by 2030, including nature-based solutions and biodiversity protection. In 2025, California also advanced a partnership with the State of Pará to strengthen cooperation on wildfire prevention and response — enhancing forest monitoring, identifying areas most at risk, and sharing research and expertise to improve firefighting and emergency management. 

 Kenya (2025): California signed a partnership focused on cutting pollution and supporting trade. The partnership advances medium- and long-term low-carbon development , policy research, development, and innovation in sustainable land use and urban planning that reduces long commutes and urban sprawl, while promoting integrated land use and transport systems. 

 Noord-Holland (2024): California and Noord-Holland signed a Letter of Intent advancing next-generation air mobility — from drones to zero-emission aircraft. Joint innovation missions are producing pilot projects that inform California’s Advanced Air Mobility Implementation Plan and readiness for major global events.

 Australia (2023): California signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) with Australia that helped inform the country’s first-ever vehicle carbon emissions standards through input from the California Air Resources Board. The California Public Utilities Commission and California ISO have also advised Australia on electricity market reform to better align incentives for renewable energy.

 British Columbia (2023): California and British Columbia signed a memorandum of understanding on mutual wildfire assistance that is delivering results. British Columbia sent incident management experts to support California’s Palisades Fire in 2025, while CAL FIRE deployed personnel during British Columbia’s 2025 fire season. These exchanges established a lasting framework for cross-border wildfire support.

 China (2023): California signed five Memoranda of Understanding (MOUs) with China’s National Development and Reform Commission, the provinces of Guangdong and Jiangsu, and the municipalities of Beijing and Shanghai to advance cooperation in cutting greenhouse gas emissions, transitioning away from fossil fuels, and developing clean energy.

 Denmark (2021): California and Denmark signed a memorandum of understanding to collaborate on groundwater mapping, leak detection, and water efficiency, which has modernized California’s data systems and informed key state programs, like the Airborne Electromagnetic Survey. Danish technologies and expertise have helped strengthen drought and water-supply resilience statewide.

 Mexico (Baja California & Sonora): California signed Memoranda of Understanding (MOUs) with the Mexican states of Baja California and Sonora to advance zero-emission freight corridors, clean ports, and battery manufacturing — strengthening North American supply chains and workforce readiness. Joint forums have already produced new research collaborations and training programs advancing clean-tech.

 California’s clean energy leadership

 Since Governor Newsom took office in 2019, California has added more than 37,000 megawatts of utility-scale clean and renewable energy to serve the California grid — and battery storage has ramped up from fewer than 700 MW to more than 21,000 MW , helping make the grid more reliable and pushing the state further along its clean energy transition. 
 Batteries play a key role in California’s goal of getting all of its electricity from clean sources by 2045. The most recent numbers, from the end of 2024, show real progress: 67% of retail electricity sales in the state already come from clean energy. Last year, clean energy met 100% of the state’s electricity needs for at least part of the day on 279 separate days. So far in 2026, that’s happened on more than nine out of 10 days during the first half of the year.

 Clean energy is also good for the economy. California leads the nation in total clean energy jobs, with 552,300 workers employed across clean energy technologies, nearly twice as many as the second-ranked state, Texas, according to a 2025 report from E2 . California’s clean energy workforce grew by nearly 7,300 workers in 2024, outpacing job growth in the rest of the state’s economy by more than three times.

 NEW YORK CITY – Governor Gavin Newsom today opened California’s participation at Climate Week NYC by meeting with international leaders and announcing new partnerships to advance clean energy, strengthen energy security, and prepare for the impacts of climate change. 

 A key announcement from the day was a new Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with Spain. Governor Newsom joined Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez and Deputy Prime Minister Sara Aagesen to sign the MOU, which expands cooperation on clean energy, electrification, battery storage, carbon markets, methane reduction, climate resilience, and sustainable development.

 Strengthening global climate leadership

 At America Is All In’s Local to Global Exchange , Governor Newsom participated in a fireside chat moderated by Antha Williams of Bloomberg Philanthropies, alongside European Commissioner for Climate, Net Zero and Clean Growth Wopke Hoekstra. The conversation focused on how California and the European Union can deepen collaboration to accelerate clean energy deployment, strengthen energy security and economic competitiveness, build resilience to worsening climate impacts, and advance carbon markets and climate innovation.

 The Governor highlighted California’s experience managing the growing impacts of climate change, including increasingly severe extreme heat, drought, flooding, wildfire, and coastal hazards. California has experienced two worst-in-a-millennium droughts in the past 15 years, followed by the wettest three-week period in the state’s history. The Governor and Commissioner Hoekstra acknowledged the hottest summer on record, including Europe’s summer of extreme heat , which claimed tens of thousands of lives and placed severe pressure on communities and critical infrastructure across the continent.

 California is investing in earlier preparation and stronger resilience. This summer, the state released an updated Extreme Heat Action Plan and expanded its heat tool — CalHeatScore — to provide communities with real-time, ZIP-code-level information about heat risk. Yesterday, Governor Newsom also proclaimed a state of emergency to streamline preparations for a historic El Niño and support communities and state agencies responding to heightened risks of flooding, coastal erosion, and severe storms.

 The Governor and the Commissioner also discussed the growing convergence of climate, energy security, and economic competitiveness. As Trump’s war with Iran continues rattling volatile global fossil fuel markets, California and Europe are accelerating electrification and clean energy deployment to strengthen energy independence, protect consumers, and build more resilient economies. At the same time, China is moving aggressively to dominate the clean energy economy. The Governor and Commissioner both warned that California and our partners cannot afford to cede the industries, jobs, and supply chains that will define the next generation of the global economy. 

 The conversation also underscored the urgency of continued climate action as the world approaches a period when, as the UN warned earlier this month, temporarily exceeding 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) of warming is increasingly difficult to avoid.

 Strengthening California subnational climate cooperation

 During Climate Week NYC, Governor Newsom engaged with European leaders to advance continued partnership on climate action, clean energy, and economic growth.

 Germany 
Governor Newsom met with German Federal Environment Minister Carsten Schneider to discuss opportunities to deepen California-Germany cooperation on clean energy, climate action, and shared economic opportunity. The Governor was joined by Yana Garcia, Secretary of the California Environmental Protection Agency, and David Hochschild, Chair of the California Energy Commission.

 California and Germany have already collaborated through key international climate and clean-energy initiatives, including the Global Offshore Wind Alliance, the ZEV Transition Council, and the International Carbon Action Partnership. California and the German state of Baden-Württemberg are also co-founders of the Under2 Coalition and members of the Subnational Methane Action Coalition.

 The group discussed a wide range of bilateral issues on climate, including implementing electric vehicle incentives, expanding battery storage to strengthen grid reliability, and competing with China in green energy and zero-emission vehicle production.

 Spain 
Governor Newsom also met with Spanish President Pedro Sánchez and Third Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Ecological Transition and Demographic Challenge Sara Aagesen to sign a new Memorandum of Understanding strengthening California-Spain collaboration on climate action and clean energy.

 The MOU advances cooperation on clean energy and electrification, climate resilience and adaptation, carbon markets, methane reductions, the circular economy, and resilient buildings and urban design.

 California and Spain share a commitment to scaling renewable energy and battery storage, strengthening grid reliability, preparing for extreme heat and wildfire, and ensuring the clean-energy transition delivers benefits for communities, workers, and businesses.

 Supporting healthy communities

 Governor Newsom also joined First Partner Jennifer Siebel Newsom at the Alice Waters Institute’s annual lunch honoring the Farm-to-School movement. The First Partner highlighted California’s work to connect students with fresh, nutritious meals while supporting local farmers, producers, and regional economies.

 Nearly 3 million California students are benefiting from California’s Farm to School programs . Championed by the First Partner and in partnership with the Legislature, Governor Newsom signed legislation to permanently fund California’s program, ensuring schools can continue serving students healthy meals made with California-grown ingredients.

 Farm to School investments support communities beyond the cafeteria. Every $1 invested through California Department of Food and Agriculture Farm to School farmer grants generates an estimated $2.01 in economic activity, helping strengthen local food systems and support California growers and producers.

 California at Climate Week NYC

 Climate Week NYC convenes government leaders, businesses, investors, advocates, researchers, philanthropies, and community leaders from around the world to advance practical climate solutions.

 Governor Newsom is participating to highlight California’s record of cutting pollution while growing the economy, strengthen partnerships with international and subnational leaders, and accelerate progress on clean energy, zero-emission transportation, climate resilience, and economic opportunity.

 California’s global climate network

 California has long been a key player on the international stage — from taking joint action on climate change to identifying new pathways and partnerships for sustained economic growth. During the Newsom administration alone, California has formed over 70 international partnerships that lay critical groundwork for our continued economic success, while prioritizing workers and businesses that benefit from these new opportunities.

 Golden State and global partnerships 

 United Kingdom (2026): California and the United Kingdom signed a memorandum of understanding to tackle climate change and promote sustainable development together. The memorandum of understanding builds on an already strong history of cooperation, and focuses on areas for collaboration including clean energy technologies, climate resilience, decarbonizing transportation, and protecting the natural environment. 

 Chile (2025): California and Chile signed a memorandum of understanding regarding exchanging information, developing best practices, and cooperating on methane emissions reduction. Methane is a highly potent greenhouse gas, and the partnership between California and Chile opens up new opportunities for both partners to cooperate on methane reduction in waste, agriculture, and energy sectors.

 Colombia (2025): California and Colombia signed a partnership to advance joint efforts on forest conservation , methane reduction, climate resilience, and clean energy development. The memorandum of understanding deepens coordination on protecting the Amazon, strengthening biodiversity, and expanding nature-based climate solutions that support sustainable and equitable economic growth.

 Nigeria (2025): California signed a memorandum of understanding with Nigeria on sustainable urban transportation, green ports, low-carbon transportation fuels, climate adaptation, methane detection and abatement policies, greenhouse gas emissions and air quality, and academic exchange and university partnerships. The partnership will build upon our shared commitment to sustainable growth, accelerate the transition to zero-emission transportation, and expand opportunities for the next generation.

 Brazil (2025): California signed a memorandum of understanding with the Brazilian federal government to scale up cooperation on climate, clean energy, cutting pollution, and job-creating climate opportunities. This new partnership, announced in September 2025, will advance market-based carbon pricing programs, expand clean transportation, including zero-emission vehicles and low-carbon fuels, and strengthen air quality management through enhanced monitoring and regulatory controls. The partnership also focuses on conserving 30% of lands and coastal waters by 2030, including nature-based solutions and biodiversity protection. In 2025, California also advanced a partnership with the State of Pará to strengthen cooperation on wildfire prevention and response — enhancing forest monitoring, identifying areas most at risk, and sharing research and expertise to improve firefighting and emergency management. 

 Kenya (2025): California signed a partnership focused on cutting pollution and supporting trade. The partnership advances medium- and long-term low-carbon development , policy research, development, and innovation in sustainable land use and urban planning that reduces long commutes and urban sprawl, while promoting integrated land use and transport systems. 

 Noord-Holland (2024): California and Noord-Holland signed a Letter of Intent advancing next-generation air mobility — from drones to zero-emission aircraft. Joint innovation missions are producing pilot projects that inform California’s Advanced Air Mobility Implementation Plan and readiness for major global events.

 Australia (2023): California signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) with Australia that helped inform the country’s first-ever vehicle emissions standards through input from the California Air Resources Board. The California Public Utilities Commission and California ISO have also advised Australia on electricity market reform to better align incentives for renewable energy.

 British Columbia (2023): California and British Columbia signed a memorandum of understanding on mutual wildfire assistance that is delivering results. British Columbia sent incident management experts to support California’s Palisades Fire in 2025, while CAL FIRE deployed personnel during British Columbia’s 2025 fire season. These exchanges established a lasting framework for cross-border wildfire support.

 China (2023): California signed five Memoranda of Understanding (MOUs) with China’s National Development and Reform Commission, the provinces of Guangdong and Jiangsu, and the municipalities of Beijing and Shanghai to advance cooperation in cutting greenhouse gas emissions, transitioning away from fossil fuels, and developing clean energy.

 Denmark (2021): California and Denmark signed a memorandum of understanding to collaborate on groundwater mapping, leak detection, and water efficiency, which has modernized California’s data systems and informed key state programs, like the Airborne Electromagnetic Survey. Danish technologies and expertise have helped strengthen drought and water-supply resilience statewide.

 Mexico (Baja California & Sonora): California signed Memoranda of Understanding (MOUs) with the Mexican states of Baja California and Sonora to advance zero-emission freight corridors, clean ports, and battery manufacturing — strengthening North American supply chains and workforce readiness. Joint forums have already produced new research collaborations and training programs advancing clean-tech.

 California’s clean energy leadership

 Since Governor Newsom took office in 2019, California has added more than 37,000 megawatts of utility-scale clean and renewable energy to serve the California grid — and battery storage has ramped up from fewer than 700 MW to more than 21,000 MW , helping make the grid more reliable and pushing the state further along its clean energy transition.

 Batteries play a key role in California’s goal of getting all of its electricity from clean sources by 2045. The most recent numbers, from the end of 2024, show real progress: 67% of retail electricity sales in the state already come from clean energy. Last year, clean energy met 100% of the state’s electricity needs for at least part of the day on 279 separate days. So far in 2026, that’s happened on more than nine out of 10 days during the first half of the year.

 Clean energy is also good for the economy. California leads the nation in total clean energy jobs, with 552,300 workers employed across clean energy technologies, nearly twice as many as the second-ranked state, Texas, according to a 2025 report from E2 . California’s clean energy workforce grew by nearly 7,300 workers in 2024, outpacing job growth in the rest of the state’s economy by more than three times.
